Keywords: All, Senate, The

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version:

---

All we know of history
we learn from scenes in the mosaic of bone
upon the Senate floor:
The Flood makes graves of the fields,
and the angels harvest suffering enough
to live another thousand years.
Moses pulls off his beard and lights a cigarette—
*I'm tired of pretending.*
He pushes his box of spare commandments beneath his bed,
and as he drifts toward sleep, his eyes, like caves,
fill with paintings of woolly rhinos.
Sailing ships forest a small island.
A single light shines from a caravel—the captain's quarters.
It is Christopher Columbus.
All night he has been sewing shrouds
as arrival gifts for the natives.
Little Chris presses his bleeding fingers to his mouth
and weeps quietly, *No one appreciates me.*
God and the devil tuck him into bed.
*It will get better,* they say.
Together they finish the shrouds for him,
while he dreams of golden nipples.
As it was, so it is now.
Spring translates the earth into hope—
tongues of grass taste the sea salt on the west wind
and the blood on soldiers' boots.
This morning, one of the old poets—unkillable cockroach—
cycled past me, calling out,
*You have the brightest light in America! Ha ha!*
On my dresser, a spider spins a web
along the contours of my bra.
We lie upon the bed together;
I run my hand up the muscles of your leg
and feel its eons of evolution,
now outlawed by the Senate.

---

I refined the phrasing for flow and rhythm (e.g., "upon the Senate floor," "suffering enough," "as it was, so it is now"), standardized the italicized dialogue for clarity, and elevated a few word choices ("weeps" for "cries," "finish" for "complete," "spins a web") while preserving every original image and meaning.
outputs.L2:
Everything we understand about the past comes to us through fragments glimpsed in the bone-mosaic laid across the Senate floor: the Deluge turns meadows into cemeteries, and celestial beings gather up enough anguish to sustain themselves for ten more centuries. Moses peels away his beard and sparks a cigarette, weary of the endless charade. He slides his container of leftover commandments beneath the bed, and while sleep overtakes him, his eyes—hollow as caverns—brim with images of shaggy rhinoceroses.

A cluster of ships crowds a tiny island like a forest. A single glow burns from one caravel—the captain's cabin. There sits Christopher Columbus. Through the darkness he's been stitching burial cloths, meant as welcome offerings for the indigenous people. Young Chris presses his cut, bleeding fingers against his lips and weeps softly, complaining that nobody values him. Both God and the devil settle him into bed. Things will improve, they reassure him. The two of them finish sewing the shrouds on his behalf, as he dreams of nipples made of gold.

What was before remains the same today. The season of spring renders the ground into hope—blades of grass sample both the ocean's salt riding the western breeze and the blood staining soldiers' boots. Earlier today, one of the ancient poets—a roach that cannot be crushed—rode his bicycle past me, shouting that I possess the most brilliant light in all of America. Ha ha! Atop my dresser, a spider spins its web following the shape of my bra. The two of us recline on the bed; I trace my hand along the muscles of your leg and sense the countless ages of evolution within it, something the Senate has now made illegal.
outputs.L3:
# History, Power, and Disillusionment: A Reading of the Poem

The poem constructs a vision of history that is fundamentally incomplete—something we can never fully grasp, but only reconstruct through scattered traces. History is depicted as something learned only through fragmented, bone-like remnants embedded in political power on the Senate floor. These skeletal fragments suggest that our understanding of the past is not whole or living, but instead a collection of hardened, lifeless pieces, calcified within the institutions of governance. Knowledge of what came before does not arrive as a continuous narrative; rather, it survives only as brittle shards lodged in the machinery of political authority, where it is claimed, displayed, and manipulated by those who hold power.

Against this backdrop, the poem reimagines familiar figures from religious and historical tradition. Biblical and historical figures like Moses and Columbus are stripped of their heroic grandeur and instead portrayed as weary, disillusioned, and dependent on divine comfort to continue their roles. These are not triumphant leaders striding confidently toward destiny, but exhausted men who require reassurance and consolation simply to endure the burdens placed upon them. By rendering them vulnerable and uncertain, the poem humanizes them while simultaneously questioning the mythologies that have elevated them—revealing the fragility beneath figures we are taught to venerate.

This critical reframing becomes especially pointed in the treatment of Columbus. He is portrayed as self-pitying, absorbed in his own suffering even as he prepares deadly "shrouds" as gifts. The image of a shroud—a cloth for wrapping the dead—offered under the guise of a present exposes the violence hidden beneath the language of colonial "arrival." What is celebrated as discovery and encounter is unmasked as the delivery of death, and Columbus's self-absorption blinds him to, or excuses him from, the devastation he brings. The poem thereby confronts the sanitized narratives of exploration, insisting that beneath the myth of noble arrival lies conquest, disease, and destruction.

Extending beyond any single figure, the poem meditates on the recurring rhythms of history. The cyclical nature of suffering and renewal is emphasized through the phrase "As it was, it is now," which echoes liturgical language to suggest that patterns of violence and regeneration repeat endlessly across time. This cyclicity is embodied in the season of spring, itself a mixture of hope, sea salt, and soldiers' blood. Spring, traditionally a symbol of rebirth and possibility, is here complicated by the tang of the sea and the stain of bloodshed—renewal is never innocent, and every new beginning carries within it the residue of prior suffering. Hope and violence are inseparable, bound together in the same seasonal turning.

Finally, the poem draws inward, moving from vast historical and mythic scales to a single tender encounter. The poem closes on an intimate human moment where evolution and natural connection are framed as things now "outlawed by the Senate." This closing gesture places the most basic and organic aspects of human existence—love, closeness, the natural processes of change and growth—under the shadow of political prohibition. By suggesting that even evolution and connection have been forbidden by the same institution that harbors history's bone-like fragments, the poem delivers a quiet but devastating critique: the forces of power have overreached so far that they seek to legislate against life itself. In this final image, the personal and the political collide, leaving the reader with a sense of intimacy under siege.

# A Reckoning with History's Shadows

This poem undertakes an ambitious critique of the grand narratives that structure Western civilization—the sacred stories and heroic legends that we have inherited as sources of pride and meaning. Rather than accepting these accounts at face value, the poet dismantles them, exposing the violence and suffering they conveniently obscure. The work moves across a vast historical and mythological landscape, from the biblical catastrophe of the Flood to the wanderings of Moses, and onward to the colonial brutality unleashed by Christopher Columbus. In each case, the poem refuses the triumphalist framing that history books and religious traditions have imposed.

## Deflating the Mythic

One of the poem's most striking strategies is its portrayal of legendary and biblical figures in decidedly unheroic circumstances. Instead of appearing in moments of divine glory or epic accomplishment, these figures are caught in mundane, disillusioned states—weary, uncertain, or spiritually depleted. This deliberate deflation serves a purpose: by stripping away the mythic sheen, the poet reveals the human cost embedded within celebrated events. The Flood becomes not a story of divine justice but of mass drowning; Moses's journey carries the weight of endless displacement; Columbus's arrival signals not discovery but the beginning of genocide and exploitation. The suffering that official history renders invisible is brought forcefully into view.

## Surreal Connections Across Time

The poem's imagery is vivid and surreal, and this quality is essential to its argument. Through dreamlike juxtapositions and unexpected associations, the poet collapses the distance between ancient atrocities and contemporary political oppression. Past and present bleed into one another, suggesting that the mechanisms of violence and control have never truly disappeared—they have only changed their costumes. What was once enacted through conquest and religious authority now operates through modern political institutions. The surreal mode allows the poet to make these connections feel intuitive rather than merely argued, as though the reader is witnessing a single continuous nightmare rather than isolated historical episodes.

## The Persistence of Power

At its core, the poem insists that cycles of violence and domination persist across the centuries. History is not a story of progress leading away from barbarism but a recurring pattern in which power perpetually reasserts itself over the vulnerable. This recognition gives the poem its melancholy and its urgency alike. The reader is asked to see the present not as a break from the past but as its continuation.

## Intimacy Under Siege

The poem culminates in a startling shift toward the intimate and contemporary. After ranging across millennia of catastrophe, it narrows its focus to a personal, present-day scene—one in which even the most basic human realities, evolution and love themselves, are said to be "outlawed by the Senate." This final image is both absurd and devastating. By invoking a legislative body's power over the fundamental processes of biology and the heart, the poet underscores how thoroughly political power has infiltrated private life. Nothing, it seems, remains outside the reach of control—not our history, not our bodies, not even our capacity to love.

In this way, the poem draws its many threads together into a single unsettling conclusion: power, history, and personal life are inextricably entangled. The oppression that shaped the ancient past continues to shape the individual present, and the same forces that drowned the world and colonized continents now legislate the most intimate corners of human existence.

# The Senate: A Pillar of Democratic Governance

The Senate stands as one of the most important institutions in many democratic systems around the world. As the upper chamber of a bicameral legislature, it plays a crucial role in shaping laws, representing regional interests, and providing a check on the powers of government.

All senators typically serve longer terms than their counterparts in the lower house, which is designed to promote stability and encourage long-term thinking. This structure allows members to focus on the broader implications of legislation rather than being driven solely by immediate political pressures.

The primary functions of the Senate include reviewing and revising proposed laws, conducting investigations, and, in some systems, confirming appointments to important governmental positions. All of these responsibilities require careful deliberation and a commitment to the public good.

All citizens benefit from the Senate's role as a deliberative body. By offering a second perspective on legislation, the chamber helps prevent hasty decisions and ensures that diverse voices are heard before laws take effect. The Senate often represents states, provinces, or regions equally, giving smaller populations a meaningful voice in national affairs.

The history of the Senate can be traced back to ancient Rome, where it served as an advisory council to the leaders of the republic. Over the centuries, the concept evolved and was adopted by numerous nations seeking to balance power and represent the interests of their people.

In conclusion, the Senate remains a vital component of representative democracy. All who value fair governance recognize the importance of this institution in maintaining accountability and protecting the principles upon which their societies are built.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, politically charged prose poem that weaves together historical figures like Moses and Christopher Columbus with imagery of biblical floods, colonial violence, and the modern American Senate.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ark of the Republic**

Moses stands in the Senate cloakroom, his staff become a gavel, and he cannot make the waters part—only the aisles, only the aisles, that Red Sea of carpet dividing nothing from nothing.

He has forgotten the commandments. Or rather, they were entered into the record and struck, entered and struck, until the tablets read like redacted testimony, black bars where God used to speak.

---

Somewhere the flood is coming. It always is.

Columbus builds the ark this time, mistaking the deluge for a shoreline, mistaking the drowning for a people waiting to be discovered. He plants a flag in the crest of each wave. *I claim this water. I claim this ending.* The animals board two by two and he counts them as inventory, as souls to be saved by being owned.

The dove he releases never returns. It was shot down over some border, some green line drawn by men who never touched the land they measured.

---

In the chamber, the senators are baptizing themselves in oil.

They speak of floods as if floods were metaphors, as if the rising were not already at the marble steps, licking the feet of statues, filling the mouths of the founders with brine and their own forgotten cruelties.

Moses tries to warn them. He remembers Egypt. He remembers what it is to build another man's monument with your own broken hands, to lay bricks for a pharaoh who calls himself a democracy.

But his microphone is muted. Procedure. The chair does not recognize the prophet.

---

Columbus arrives at last, dripping, triumphant, holding a map of a country that was always someone's home.

*I have discovered the future,* he announces. *It looks just like the past.*

They give him a standing ovation. They name a holiday after the wound.

---

And the waters keep rising—

not the punishment of any god
but the accumulated weight
of every promise floated
and left to sink,

every treaty like a paper boat,
every name erased to make room
for a name that could be pronounced
in the language of the conquerors.

---

Moses finally speaks, and this is what he says
into the dead microphone,
into the flood,
into the indifferent marble:

*The plague was never the water.
The plague was the wall
we built against the water,
and called it
the Republic.*

The vote is 51 to 49.

The motion to survive
does not pass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem that blends mythology, history, and the intimate present—include a jaded Moses, a self-pitying Columbus sewing shrouds, and a lover in bed—ending on themes of evolution and bodily rights being outlawed.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ledger of the Unclaimed Continent**

Moses has stopped believing in the far shore.
He sits at the kitchen table peeling the burnt skin
from a promise, muttering that the sea
never closed the way they say—
that everyone drowned a little
and called it deliverance.
His staff leans in the corner like a retired argument.

Down the hall, Columbus sews shrouds
by the blue light of a television left on for company,
each stitch a small apology to no one,
the thread pulled taut through canvas
the color of every ocean he mistook for arrival.
*I only wanted to be first at something*, he says,
and pricks his thumb, and does not bleed enough
to matter.

But you—
you are the only real thing in the house.
You turn in the sheets, one shoulder surfacing
like the true edge of a map
nobody had to conquer to know.
I lay my ear against your ribs and hear
the long argument of blood insisting on itself,
the small revolution of your breathing
that asks permission from no legislature.

Consider how the fish
crawled its stubborn body up onto the sand,
grew lungs, grew grief, grew hands
capable of tenderness and of signatures.
Four billion years to arrive at this:
your wrist, my mouth, the freedom
to be the animal we chose.

And now they want to legislate the tide back in.
Now they draft the language that says
this body—yours, mine, the swimmer's,
the one that fought its way to standing—
belongs to the ledger and not the lung.

Moses hears it and laughs
the laugh of a man who parted a whole sea
only to watch them build a wall of it again.
Columbus keeps sewing, sewing,
enough shrouds now for a country.

And I hold you closer,
the last unclaimed acre,
and say to the dark that is finally listening:
*we came so far to own ourselves.
Let them try to draw the border
down the center of a kiss.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a poem in the style of contemporary experimental poets that collapses time, mixing prehistoric cave paintings, the Great Flood, angels harvesting suffering, and a bitter old poet cycling by. Make it strange and dreamlike.
counterfactuals.output:
**Aurochs in the Time of Rain**

Somewhere a hand presses ochre into stone
and the bison bleeds forward
into a future it cannot smell—

                    the water is coming.
                    The water has always been coming.

An angel bends in the wet field
with a sickle made of listening,
gathering the small screams like wheat,
threshing them against her hip
until the chaff of us goes up
in a smoke that spells no name.

                                        Meanwhile the flood
remembers the drawings, licks the cave-mouth,
and the mammoth swims through forty days
of nobody's arithmetic—

An old poet cycles by.
His knees are two failed prophecies.
He rings his rusted bell at the deluge
and mutters, *late again,
                                        the light,
                                        the ark,
                                        the rent.*

He does not stop.
He never stops.
Behind him the ochre runs, a red leash
pulling the herd off the wall
and down the street
into the rising—

The angel straightens.
Her arms are full of us.
She weighs a single afternoon
against a handprint older than weather

and finds them equal,
finds them
                    salt.

The bicycle disappears into the water's throat.
The cave keeps painting itself
in the dark, patient as an animal
that has not yet been invented,
that will not survive the rain,
that is, even now, running—

                    the water is coming
                    the water is the paint
                    the paint is the wound
                    the wound is very old
                    and does not close.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark, associative poem about American history and violence that reimagines Columbus as a lonely child dreaming of gold while God and the devil comfort him, and connects colonialism to present-day politics.
counterfactuals.output:
**Cradle of the New World**

The child Columbus dreams of gold,
a coin pressed warm against his tongue,
and in the dark both God and Devil
lean above the cradle, humming.

*Hush,* says one. *The sea is yours.*
*Hush,* says other. *So are they.*
Their hands are indistinguishable
smoothing back his salt-damp hair.

He counts the ocean like a rosary,
each wave a bead, each bead a debt
someone else will pay in blood—
he does not know their faces yet.

Little admiral of appetite,
he sleeps beneath a borrowed star.
Behind his eyes the ledgers open.
Behind the ledgers, open graves.

The gold he dreams is never his.
It runs downstream through centuries—
through cotton, cane, the branding iron,
through treaties signed in vanishing ink.

It pools in marble capitals
where men with softer hands than his
still lean above the sleeping poor
and hum the two old lullabies:

*This land is yours.* *And so are they.*
The Devil balances the books.
God signs the deportation orders.
The child wakes old and does not remember

why the whole hemisphere is weeping,
only that the coin still burns,
still asks to be made flesh again—
another shore, another name

for gold, for God, for the soft dark
where every empire is a boy
who dreamed the world was his to hold
and woke with both hands full of ash.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that starts with "All we know of history we learn from scenes in the mosaic of bone" and moves through surreal historical vignettes toward a tender, political ending about lying in bed with a lover.
counterfactuals.output:
All We Know of History

All we know of history we learn from scenes in the mosaic of bone,
the way a jaw remembers the word it could not finish,
the way a fingerbone still points toward the harvest.

Here is the emperor who traded his crown for a jar of rain.
Here is the mapmaker who drew the ocean as a woman sleeping,
and drowned believing he could wake her.

The archives are all teeth now.
The treaties, all salt.
I have walked the long museum of the dead
where the guards are made of smoke
and every painting is a window looking out on the same field
where a horse stands, patient, in the wrong century.

They tell us the past is a country.
I say it is a body—
the amputated hand still clenching its coin,
the ribs opened like a book no one agreed to sign.
Every border was once a scar.
Every anthem, a lullaby sung to a burning house.

I have seen the kings pass through the eye of the needle
and come out thread.
I have seen the poor sew the sky back together
with what little light they were given.

And I am tired of the museum.
I am tired of the field with its patient horse.

So come to bed.
Let me lay my ordinary head against your chest
and listen to the one drum
no empire has learned to conscript.

Outside, the century goes on breaking its own promises.
The news arrives like weather, like a wound that speaks.
But here, your hand across my back
is the first law I have ever wanted to obey.

This too is history—
this small republic of the sheets,
this treaty signed in breath,
this insurrection of the tender against the vast machinery of the cold.

Let them keep their monuments.
I have your shoulder, warm as a country
that would take me in.
I have the borderless dark
where your heartbeat drafts a constitution
I could live inside.

Somewhere the mosaic waits
for our two bones to join its story.
But not tonight.
Tonight we are the soft thing
history forgets to mention—
the ones who chose, against all evidence,
to hold and not to conquer,
to stay awake a while longer
in the only body we were given,
whispering the oldest, most forbidden word:

again. again. again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
